problem:
Given a sorted list of distinct integers nums and an integer target, return the index of target in nums, or -1 if it is not present. Your algorithm must run in O(log n) time.

Example: nums = [-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12], target = 9 -> 4
Example: nums = [-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12], target = 2 -> -1

data.generator_code:
def generate(rng, n):
    n = max(1, n)
    nums = sorted(rng.sample(range(-10000, 10000), n))
    target = rng.choice(nums) if rng.random() > 0.5 else rng.randint(-10000, 10000)
    if target not in nums and rng.random() > 0.5 and n > 0:
        target = nums[0] - 1
    return [nums, target]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    n = max(1, n)
    nums = list(range(n))
    target = -99999
    return [nums, target]

data.key_insight: Since the array is sorted, we can repeatedly divide the search space in half by comparing the target with the middle element.

steps.title: Initialize Pointers
steps.detail: Set the left pointer to 0 and the right pointer to the last index of the array.

steps.title: Iterate While Search Space is Valid
steps.detail: While left <= right, calculate the middle index to avoid overflow as mid = left + (right - left) // 2.

steps.title: Compare Middle Element
steps.detail: If nums[mid] equals target, return mid. If nums[mid] < target, move left to mid + 1. Otherwise, move right to mid - 1.

steps.title: Target Not Found
steps.detail: If the loop terminates without finding the target, return -1.

data.pattern_summary: Binary search is used to find an item in a sorted collection by repeatedly halving the search space, reducing time complexity from linear to logarithmic.

pattern_options.name: Binary Search
pattern_options.feedback: This fits because the array is sorted and we need an O(log n) search time.

pattern_options.name: Linear Scan
pattern_options.feedback: A linear scan checks every element one by one, which takes O(n) time and violates the time complexity requirement.

pattern_options.name: Two Pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers usually work well on sorted arrays for pairs or subarrays, but a single target lookup does not require two moving endpoints.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Building a hash map takes O(n) time and O(n) space, which violates the O(log n) time requirement without utilizing the existing sorted order.

signals.hint: Implies that the elements have a predictable order, meaning we can rule out large chunks of data at once.

signals.phrase: must run in O(log n) time
signals.hint: Rules out checking every element one by one and requires an approach that cuts the problem size in half at each step.

data.brute_force_idea: Iterate through every element in the list from left to right, comparing each element to the target until a match is found or the end of the list is reached.
data.brute_force_why: In the worst case, every single element in the list must be checked once.
data.bottleneck: Checking each element one by one ignores the sorted property of the list, forcing the algorithm to look at elements that could have been skipped.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many elements are inspected when the target is at the very end of a large list.
Consider how the sorted property could tell you whether to look left or right without checking every value.
Think about how dividing the remaining elements in half at each step would change the number of checks.

data.overview: Binary search efficiently finds the index of a target value in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search space. It achieves logarithmic time complexity by discarding half of the remaining elements at each step.
data.intuition: Imagine looking up a word in a physical dictionary. You open it to the middle; if your word is alphabetically later, you tear off and throw away the entire left half, repeating until you find the exact word.

pitfalls: Forgetting to include the equals sign in 'left <= right', which causes infinite loops or missed single-element checks.
Calculating mid as (left + right) // 2 which can lead to integer overflow in other languages.
Failing to update left or right properly by adding or subtracting 1, leading to infinite loops.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach checks every element one by one, leading to linear time. The optimized approach leverages the fact that the array is sorted. By calculating the midpoint and discarding half of the remaining elements at each step, it narrows down the search space exponentially.

derivation.note: The while loop runs as the search space is halved each iteration.
Performs basic arithmetic to find the midpoint.
Compares the middle element to the target once per iteration.
Updates the left boundary in constant time.
Updates the right boundary in constant time.

data.time_summary: Line 6 runs log n times based on the measured evidence (n=4 takes 3 loop steps, n=8 takes 4, n=16 takes 5, and n=32 takes 6). Inside the loop, lines 7, 8, and 10/13 execute once per iteration in O(1) time. Multiplying the loop iterations by the constant-time operations inside gives O(log n) total time.
data.space_summary: Only a few scalar integer variables (left, right, mid) are maintained, using O(1) extra memory regardless of input size.
data.takeaway: When an array is sorted and you need to find an element, eliminate half the remaining candidates at each step by comparing against the middle element.
mistakes: Forgetting to update left or right relative to mid, leading to infinite loops.
Using left + right instead of left + (right - left) // 2, which can cause integer overflow in other languages.
Off-by-one errors in boundary initializations like setting right = len(nums).
